blocks.en: Why Appreciate Biblical Languages?

blocks.en: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
blocks.es_reference: «En el principio era el Verbo, y el Verbo era con Dios, y el Verbo era Dios».

blocks.en: Course Scripture: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that was made." — John 1:1–3 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Escritura del Curso: «En el principio era el Verbo, y el Verbo era con Dios, y el Verbo era Dios. Este era en el principio con Dios. Todas las cosas por él fueron hechas, y sin él nada de lo que ha sido hecho, fue hecho». — Juan 1:1–3 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation: The Day Helen Keller Found the Word "Water"
blocks.es_reference: Orientación: El día que Helen Keller encontró la palabra «agua»

blocks.en: Helen Keller was nineteen months old when an illness left her deaf and blind. For five years she lived in a silent darkness no one could reach. She had hand signs for "father" and "bread," but no idea that a thing called a word even existed.
blocks.es_reference: Helen Keller tenía diecinueve meses cuando una enfermedad la dejó sorda y ciega. Durante cinco años vivió en una oscuridad silenciosa que nadie podía alcanzar. Tenía señas de mano para «padre» y «pan», pero ninguna idea de que algo llamado palabra existiera.

blocks.en: When she was six, a teacher named Anne Sullivan came to her. For weeks Anne spelled letters into Helen's palm — D–O–L–L for the doll, C–A–K–E for the cake — and Helen learned to mimic the finger movements without understanding they meant anything. Anne was patient. Anne kept spelling.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando tenía seis años, una maestra llamada Anne Sullivan vino a ella. Durante semanas Anne deletreó letras en la palma de Helen — M–U–Ñ–E–C–A para la muñeca, P–A–S–T–E–L para el pastel — y Helen aprendió a imitar los movimientos de los dedos sin entender que significaban algo. Anne fue paciente. Anne siguió deletreando.

blocks.en: On April 5, 1887, Anne took Helen out to the pump in the back yard. She ran cold water over one of Helen's hands while spelling W–A–T–E–R into the other. The connection clicked. Helen wrote later:
blocks.es_reference: El 5 de abril de 1887, Anne llevó a Helen a la bomba en el patio trasero. Dejó correr agua fría sobre una de las manos de Helen mientras deletreaba A–G–U–A en la otra. La conexión encajó. Helen escribió después:

blocks.en: "Suddenly I felt a misty consciousness as of something forgotten — a thrill of returning thought; and somehow the mystery of language was revealed to me. I knew then that 'w-a-t-e-r' meant the wonderful cool something that was flowing over my hand. Everything had a name, and each name gave birth to a new thought."
blocks.es_reference: «De repente sentí una conciencia brumosa como de algo olvidado — un estremecimiento del pensamiento que regresaba; y de alguna manera el misterio del lenguaje se me reveló. Supe entonces que «a-g-u-a» significaba esa maravillosa cosa fría que fluía sobre mi mano. Todo tenía un nombre, y cada nombre daba a luz un nuevo pensamiento».

blocks.en: She learned thirty words that afternoon. By the end of her life she had written fourteen books, graduated from Radcliffe, and lectured in four languages. One word taught her that words were not noise. They were doors.
blocks.es_reference: Aprendió treinta palabras esa tarde. Para el final de su vida había escrito catorce libros, se había graduado de Radcliffe, y había dado conferencias en cuatro idiomas. Una palabra le enseñó que las palabras no eran ruido. Eran puertas.

blocks.en: "Everything had a name, and each name gave birth to a new thought." — Helen Keller, on the day language broke through
blocks.es_reference: «Todo tenía un nombre, y cada nombre daba a luz un nuevo pensamiento». — Helen Keller, el día en que el lenguaje irrumpió

blocks.en: That hand at the pump is every Bible reader who has sat with a verse and felt there was more in it than the English could hold. He knows love in 1 Corinthians 13. He knows grace in Ephesians 2. He has held those English words like Helen held the doll — spelled, repeated, even preached — but somewhere underneath there is cool water he has not yet touched. The English word is the sign in the palm. The Greek or Hebrew is the water. When the two connect, verses he has read his whole life become doors.
blocks.es_reference: Esa mano en la bomba es cada lector de la Biblia que se ha sentado con un versículo y ha sentido que había más en él de lo que el castellano podía sostener. Conoce amor en 1 Corintios 13. Conoce gracia en Efesios 2. Ha sostenido esas palabras castellanas como Helen sostenía la muñeca — deletreadas, repetidas, incluso predicadas — pero en alguna parte debajo hay agua fría que todavía no ha tocado. La palabra castellana es el signo en la palma. La griega o hebrea es el agua. Cuando las dos se conectan, los versículos que ha leído toda su vida se vuelven puertas.

blocks.en: This course does not propose to make you a Greek or Hebrew scholar. It proposes something better: access. By Unit 11 you will know how to put your hand under the spout.
blocks.es_reference: Este curso no propone hacerte un erudito de griego o hebreo. Propone algo mejor: acceso. Para la Unidad 11 sabrás cómo poner tu mano bajo el caño.

blocks.en: I. Why the Original Languages Matter
blocks.es_reference: I. Por qué importan las lenguas originales

blocks.en: Modern translations are good. You can be a faithful believer, a strong pastor, and a wise saint without ever learning one Hebrew letter. Yet there is a reason the church has always trained its teachers in the original languages, a reason Tyndale and Reina and Valera were willing to die to put the Bible into the everyday tongue. Five reasons matter for this course.
blocks.es_reference: Las traducciones modernas son buenas. Puedes ser un creyente fiel, un pastor fuerte, y un santo sabio sin nunca aprender una letra hebrea. Sin embargo, hay una razón por la que la iglesia siempre ha entrenado a sus maestros en las lenguas originales, una razón por la que Tyndale y Reina y Valera estuvieron dispuestos a morir para poner la Biblia en la lengua cotidiana. Cinco razones importan para este curso.

blocks.en: <th>#</th><th>Reason</th>
blocks.es_reference: <th>#</th><th>Razón</th>

blocks.en: 1God chose specific languages. Inspiration was breathed into Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek words. The choice of language was part of the inspiration.
blocks.es_reference: 1Dios escogió idiomas específicos. La inspiración fue insuflada en palabras hebreas, arameas, y griegas. La elección del idioma fue parte de la inspiración.

blocks.en: 2No translation captures everything. Hebrew's earthiness and Greek's precision do not pour fully into English or Spanish containers. Every translation gains something and loses something.
blocks.es_reference: 2Ninguna traducción captura todo. La terrenalidad del hebreo y la precisión del griego no se vierten completamente en recipientes castellanos o ingleses. Cada traducción gana algo y pierde algo.

blocks.en: 3Word studies open doors. The English love has to cover four different Greek words. The English word has to cover the rich Greek logos. When Jesus questioned Peter three times in John 21, He used agapê and phileô — two different Greek words doing different work that the English collapses into one.
blocks.es_reference: 3Los estudios de palabras abren puertas. El castellano amor tiene que cubrir cuatro palabras griegas diferentes. El castellano verbo tiene que cubrir el rico griego logos. Cuando Jesús preguntó a Pedro tres veces en Juan 21, usó agapê y phileô — dos palabras griegas diferentes haciendo trabajos diferentes que el castellano colapsa en una.

blocks.en: 4You do not need fluency. You need access. The ability to look up any biblical word in under a minute and know what it means is enough. Access takes weeks. Fluency takes years. This course delivers access.
blocks.es_reference: 4No necesitas fluidez. Necesitas acceso. La habilidad de buscar cualquier palabra bíblica en menos de un minuto y saber lo que significa es suficiente. El acceso toma semanas. La fluidez toma años. Este curso entrega acceso.

blocks.en: 5The seminary wall has fallen. James Strong's 1890 Concordance handed the keys to every layman. Free apps (Blue Letter Bible, Bible Hub) have finished what Strong began. Anyone with a phone can now do what only a Greek professor could do a hundred and fifty years ago.
blocks.es_reference: 5La pared del seminario ha caído. La Concordancia de James Strong de 1890 entregó las llaves a cada laico. Las aplicaciones gratuitas (Blue Letter Bible, Bible Hub) han terminado lo que Strong comenzó. Cualquiera con un teléfono puede hacer hoy lo que solo un profesor de griego podía hacer hace ciento cincuenta años.

blocks.en: II. The Three Biblical Languages: A Map
blocks.es_reference: II. Las tres lenguas bíblicas: Un mapa

blocks.en: The Bible was written in three languages, not one.
blocks.es_reference: La Biblia fue escrita en tres idiomas, no uno.

blocks.en: <th>Language</th><th>Where used</th><th>Character</th>
blocks.es_reference: <th>Idioma</th><th>Dónde se usa</th><th>Carácter</th>

blocks.en: HebrewAlmost all of the Old Testament (~22,000 verses). 22 consonants, no vowel letters, read right to left.Concrete, earthy, picture-based. The language of root and soil, hand and house and door.
blocks.es_reference: HebreoCasi todo el Antiguo Testamento (~22,000 versículos). 22 consonantes, sin letras vocales, se lee de derecha a izquierda.Concreto, terrenal, basado en imágenes. La lengua de la raíz y el suelo, la mano y la casa y la puerta.

blocks.en: AramaicParts of Daniel and Ezra; phrases scattered in the New Testament. Hebrew's sister language.The everyday tongue of the Jewish people by Christ's day. Jesus spoke Aramaic.
blocks.es_reference: ArameoPartes de Daniel y Esdras; frases dispersas en el Nuevo Testamento. Lengua hermana del hebreo.La lengua cotidiana del pueblo judío para el día de Cristo. Jesús hablaba arameo.

blocks.en: GreekAll of the New Testament (~8,000 verses). 24 letters, read left to right.Koinê — the common Greek of streets and markets, not the literary Greek of Plato. The lingua franca of the Roman world.
blocks.es_reference: GriegoTodo el Nuevo Testamento (~8,000 versículos). 24 letras, se lee de izquierda a derecha.Koinê — el griego común de calles y mercados, no el griego literario de Platón. La lengua franca del mundo romano.

blocks.en: You will hear all three in the New Testament, sometimes in the same verse. Jesus cried "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?" from the cross in Aramaic (Matthew 27:46). Paul ended 1 Corinthians with "Maranatha" — Aramaic for "our Lord, come" (16:22). The apostles called God "Abba," the Aramaic word a Jewish toddler used at home (Mark 14:36, Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6). Christ Himself moved among all three.
blocks.es_reference: Oirás las tres en el Nuevo Testamento, a veces en el mismo versículo. Jesús clamó «Elí, Elí, ¿lama sabactani?» desde la cruz en arameo (Mateo 27:46). Pablo terminó 1 Corintios con «Maranata» — arameo para «nuestro Señor, ven» (16:22). Los apóstoles llamaban a Dios «Abba», la palabra aramea que un niño judío usaba en casa (Marcos 14:36, Romanos 8:15, Gálatas 4:6). Cristo mismo se movió entre las tres.

blocks.en: Hebrew is the language of root and earth. Greek is the language of precision and nuance. Aramaic is the language Christ prayed in.
blocks.es_reference: El hebreo es la lengua de la raíz y la tierra. El griego es la lengua de la precisión y el matiz. El arameo es la lengua en que Cristo oró.

blocks.en: IV. Why John 1:1 Is Our Course Scripture
blocks.es_reference: IV. Por qué Juan 1:1 es nuestra escritura del curso

blocks.en: Every course needs an anchor verse. Ours is John 1:1: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
blocks.es_reference: Cada curso necesita un versículo ancla. El nuestro es Juan 1:1: «En el principio era el Verbo, y el Verbo era con Dios, y el Verbo era Dios».

blocks.en: The Greek word for "Word" is logos — Strong's G3056, one of the four foundational Greek words you will study in Unit 8. In Greek philosophy logos meant more than a spoken syllable; it was the rational principle that holds the universe together, the logic of the cosmos. John picked up this rich word and applied it to Jesus Christ Himself: the Son of God is the Logos, the Word spoken from eternity, the rational principle behind creation walking in Galilee.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra griega para «Verbo» es logos — número de Strong G3056, una de las cuatro palabras griegas fundamentales que estudiarás en la Unidad 8. En la filosofía griega logos significaba más que una sílaba hablada; era el principio racional que sostiene unido al universo, la lógica del cosmos. Juan tomó esta rica palabra y la aplicó a Jesucristo mismo: el Hijo de Dios es el Logos, el Verbo hablado desde la eternidad, el principio racional detrás de la creación caminando en Galilea.

blocks.en: The verse anchors this course for three reasons. First, it is itself about words — God's revelation is verbal, and Christ Himself is the Word. Second, it cannot be fully understood from English or Spanish alone; the Greek opens what the translation only hints at. Third, it closes the loop: every Hebrew and Greek letter you will learn in this course is finally a road sign pointing to the same Word, who is Christ. Henrietta Mears put it simply: the Bible is one Book, one Hero, one Story. The Hero is Jesus, the Logos of John 1:1.
blocks.es_reference: El versículo ancla este curso por tres razones. Primero, trata por sí mismo de palabras — la revelación de Dios es verbal, y Cristo mismo es el Verbo. Segundo, no puede entenderse completamente desde el castellano o el inglés solos; el griego abre lo que la traducción solo insinúa. Tercero, cierra el círculo: cada letra hebrea y griega que aprenderás en este curso es finalmente una señal de camino apuntando al mismo Verbo, que es Cristo. Henrietta Mears lo dijo simplemente: la Biblia es un Libro, un Héroe, una Historia. El Héroe es Jesús, el Logos de Juan 1:1.

blocks.en: The course is about words because Christ is the Word.
blocks.es_reference: El curso trata de palabras porque Cristo es el Verbo.

blocks.en: The promise
blocks.es_reference: La promesa

blocks.en: By the end of this course you will know the Hebrew alphabet, the Greek alphabet, the meaning of about thirteen of the most important original-language words in the Bible, and how to look up any other in under a minute. You will not be a scholar. You will be a Bible reader with the door open. You will read John 1:1 and see logos. You will read Mark 14:36 and hear Abba. Like Helen Keller at the pump, you will finally feel the cool water beneath the sign you have been spelling all your life.
blocks.es_reference: Para el final de este curso conocerás el alfabeto hebreo, el alfabeto griego, el significado de unas trece de las palabras más importantes en lengua original de la Biblia, y cómo buscar cualquier otra en menos de un minuto. No serás un erudito. Serás un lector de la Biblia con la puerta abierta. Leerás Juan 1:1 y verás logos. Leerás Marcos 14:36 y oirás Abba. Como Helen Keller en la bomba, finalmente sentirás el agua fría debajo del signo que has estado deletreando toda tu vida.

blocks.en: 📚 Catalog / Catálogo

mc.stem: What happened to Helen Keller at the water pump on April 5, 1887?
options: She regained her hearing for the first time
She met Anne Sullivan for the first time
She suddenly understood that the finger letters W-A-T-E-R meant the cold liquid flowing over her hand — the moment language broke through into her silent world
She wrote her first poem
mc.why: On April 5, 1887, at the back-yard pump, Anne Sullivan ran cold water over one of Helen's hands while spelling W-A-T-E-R into the other. After weeks of mimicking the finger movements without understanding, Helen suddenly connected the sign to the substance. She wrote later that 'the mystery of language was revealed to me' and 'everything had a name.' She learned thirty words that afternoon and went on to graduate from Radcliffe, write fourteen books, and speak four languages.

mc.stem: What did Helen Keller mean when she wrote, 'Everything had a name, and each name gave birth to a new thought'?
options: That she wanted to give names to all her toys
That she had discovered language was the door to thought itself — without words she could feel but could not think, with words a whole inner world opened
That she had named the family dog
That she would become a writer
mc.why: For Helen, the breakthrough was not just learning vocabulary. It was discovering that words ARE the door to thought. Before the water moment, she felt but could not really think because she had no words to think with. After it, an entire inner world opened to her. That insight is the doorway into this course: words in our Bible are not just signs; they are doors into the doctrine and history and salvation underneath.

mc.stem: How does the Helen Keller story apply to a Bible reader studying biblical languages?
options: The reader has held the English words (love, faith, grace) like Helen held the doll — spelled and repeated — but until he touches the Greek or Hebrew underneath, he has not yet felt the 'cool water' the word actually points to
The reader must become deaf and blind to truly understand Scripture
The reader should drink water before reading the Bible
The reader should write his Bible studies in his palm
mc.why: The Helen Keller story is the orientation analogy of this whole course. The English Bible word is the sign on the palm; the Greek or Hebrew underneath is the cool water from the pump. Until the two connect, the reader has the spelling but not the substance. This course is designed to bring them together so that you can feel what the words have been pointing at all along.

mc.stem: Why is it important that God chose specific languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek) for His revelation, rather than giving the Bible as 'floating ideas'?
options: Because Hebrew is the holiest language
Because Greek is the most logical language
Because God wanted to make Bible reading difficult for everyone

Because inspiration was given as real human words in real human tongues with real semantic ranges — the choice of language was itself part of the inspiration, meaning every word the Spirit moved an apostle to write carries the meaning of that specific tongue
mc.why: The doctrine of inspiration is that the Spirit moved real human authors to write real human words in real human tongues (2 Peter 1:21, 2 Timothy 3:16). The choice of Hebrew or Greek is not a thin layer over an abstract idea; the word IS part of the inspired text. To understand what God said, we have to understand what God's chosen words mean in the languages He chose. That is why this course exists.

mc.stem: Why does every translation, no matter how good, lose some of the original meaning?
options: Because translators are dishonest

Because languages are not interchangeable codes — Hebrew's concrete earthiness and Greek's precise nuance cannot be poured fully into English or Spanish; every translation involves a thousand small choices that gain something and lose something
Because the original manuscripts have been lost
Because translations are forbidden by God
mc.why: Languages carry cultural, semantic, and grammatical weight that does not transfer perfectly across the border. The English 'love' has to handle four different Greek words (eros, philia, storgê, agapê). The English 'word' has to handle the rich Greek logos. Every translation is a faithful attempt that nevertheless cannot capture every nuance. The original is the only version where nothing has been lost in translation.

mc.stem: What are the three languages in which the Bible was originally written?
options: Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek
Latin, Greek, and English
Hebrew, Latin, and Greek
Egyptian, Hebrew, and Greek
mc.why: The Bible was written in Hebrew (almost all of the OT), Aramaic (parts of Daniel and Ezra, scattered verses elsewhere, and phrases in the NT), and Greek (all of the NT). Latin came later as the language of the Catholic Church's Vulgate translation (around AD 400), but was never an original biblical language. Knowing these three is the first map this course gives you.

mc.stem: Approximately how much of the Old Testament was written in Hebrew, and what is the rest written in?
options: About half in Hebrew, half in Greek
Entirely in Hebrew with no other language
Almost all in Hebrew, with portions in Aramaic (notably parts of Daniel and Ezra)
Half in Hebrew, half in Aramaic
mc.why: The vast majority of the Old Testament (about 22,000 of its verses) is written in Hebrew. A small but important set of passages — Daniel 2:4 through 7:28, Ezra 4:8 through 6:18 and 7:12 through 26, plus single verses in Jeremiah and Genesis — is written in Aramaic. The Aramaic portions are concentrated in Daniel and Ezra because both books deal heavily with the Babylonian and Persian courts where Aramaic was the official language.

mc.stem: In what language was the entire New Testament originally written?
options: Latin
Koinê Greek (the common Greek of the first-century Mediterranean world)
Aramaic
Classical Greek (the Greek of Plato and Aristotle)
mc.why: The entire New Testament was written in Koinê Greek — the common Greek of the streets and markets of the first-century Roman Empire, NOT the literary Greek of Plato and Aristotle. Koinê means 'common' (from the same root as koinonia, 'fellowship'). God chose the language of the plowboy and the merchant, not the language of the philosopher, to broadcast the gospel.

mc.stem: What does the word 'Koinê' mean, and why is it significant that the New Testament was written in this kind of Greek rather than classical literary Greek?
options: Koinê means 'sacred,' and it shows God preferred a special religious language
Koinê means 'ancient,' and it shows the New Testament is very old
Koinê means 'philosophical,' and it shows the apostles were educated

Koinê means 'common' — the everyday Greek of the streets and markets, the language ordinary people spoke from Spain to Persia — signaling that God sent the gospel in the tongue of common people, not in academic or sacred language
mc.why: Koinê means 'common' (the same root as koinonia, fellowship). When Alexander the Great conquered the Mediterranean in the 300s BC, his soldiers and traders spread a simplified version of Greek that became the lingua franca from Spain to Persia. By the first century, koinê was the language every ordinary person in the empire could understand. God did not give the New Testament in the learned Greek of philosophers; He gave it in the language of fishermen, soldiers, merchants, and house slaves. The gospel was always meant for the plowboy.

mc.stem: Why did God use Aramaic in some portions of the Old Testament, especially in Daniel and Ezra?
options: Because Hebrew had been forgotten
Because Aramaic is a holier language than Hebrew
Because Aramaic was the official trade and diplomatic language of the Babylonian and Persian empires, and Daniel and Ezra both deal heavily with events and decrees from those imperial courts
Because the scribes ran out of Hebrew ink
mc.why: Aramaic became the dominant trade and diplomatic language of the ancient Near East from about 700 BC onward, especially under the Babylonian and Persian empires. Daniel served in the Babylonian and Persian courts; Ezra dealt extensively with Persian royal decrees. The Aramaic portions in both books typically record official correspondence, royal proclamations, or diplomatic exchanges. The Holy Spirit preserved these portions in the original administrative language, showing God's faithfulness even in the language of the empire.

mc.stem: Which of the following are examples of Aramaic words preserved in the New Testament Greek text?
options: Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma
Abba (father), Maranatha (our Lord, come), Talitha cumi (little girl, arise), Eli Eli lama sabachthani (My God, My God, why have you forsaken me)
Alpha, beta, gamma, delta
Hosanna, hallelujah, amen, selah
mc.why: Several Aramaic words and phrases are preserved untranslated in the Greek NT, marking moments of special intimacy or intensity. Jesus prayed 'Abba' (Aramaic for 'Daddy/Father') in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). He cried 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?' from the cross (Matthew 27:46, Aramaic for 'My God, My God, why have you forsaken Me'). 'Talitha cumi' (Mark 5:41) is what He said to raise Jairus's daughter. 'Maranatha' (1 Corinthians 16:22) is the early Christian prayer 'Our Lord, come!' These Aramaic preservations are bridges across all three biblical languages in a single NT verse.

mc.stem: In which direction is Hebrew read and written, compared to Greek?
options: Hebrew is read right to left; Greek (like English and Spanish) is read left to right
Both Hebrew and Greek are read right to left
Hebrew is read top to bottom; Greek is read bottom to top
Hebrew uses no spaces; Greek uses spaces between words
mc.why: Hebrew (along with Aramaic and Arabic, its sister Semitic languages) is read and written right to left. Greek, like English and Spanish, is read left to right. When you open a Hebrew Bible, page 1 is where the back cover of an English Bible would be. The first Hebrew word of the Bible (Bereshit, 'In the beginning') is on the right side of the first page. This is a small but important orientation point as you start reading.

mc.stem: What is the central distinction the course makes between 'fluency' and 'access'?
options: Fluency means speaking the language at a coffee shop; access means writing graduate-level papers in it
Both terms mean the same thing in this course

Fluency requires years of study to become a Greek or Hebrew scholar; access is the ability to look up any biblical word in under a minute and know what it means in its verse — access is what this course delivers, fluency is not the goal
Fluency is the only kind of language knowledge that matters
mc.why: This is the single most important promise of the course. You will not learn to read Greek the way you read Spanish or English. You will not become a Hebrew speaker. You will, however, gain the ability to look up any Hebrew or Greek word in the Bible, understand what it actually means in its verse, and use that understanding to read Scripture with depth for the rest of your life. That is access, not fluency, and it is enough.

mc.stem: What event in 1890 began the modern 'democratization' of biblical language study, and what does the course mean by 'the seminary wall has fallen'?
options: The invention of the printing press
The translation of the King James Bible
The founding of the Royal Academy of Hebrew

James Strong's publication of his Exhaustive Concordance, which assigned a unique number to every Hebrew (H1–H8674) and Greek (G1–G5624) word in the Bible — for the first time, any English-speaking layman could look up the original-language word behind any English verse without knowing a single Hebrew or Greek letter
mc.why: James Strong was a professor of Hebrew and Greek at Drew Theological Seminary in New Jersey. He spent 27 years (1863–1890) compiling his Exhaustive Concordance, which numbered every Hebrew (H1–H8674) and Greek (G1–G5624) word in the KJV Bible with a unique identifier. For the first time in history, anyone with an English Bible could see the original-language word behind any English word, look it up in the back, and read the lexical definition. The wall that had separated seminary professors from common believers collapsed. Today, free apps like Blue Letter Bible and websites like Bible Hub have finished what Strong began. We cover all of this in Unit 10.

mc.stem: According to the course, what is the goal of studying biblical languages?
options: To become fluent enough to converse with native Greek and Hebrew speakers
To gain ACCESS — the ability to look up biblical words, understand what they mean in their verses, and read Scripture with depth — without needing seminary-level fluency
To impress one's congregation by quoting Greek from the pulpit
To translate the entire Bible into a new language
mc.why: The whole course is built around this distinction. Fluency takes years and is not necessary for faithful Bible reading. Access takes weeks, and it is what enables an ordinary believer to read Scripture with depth for the rest of his life. The goal is not to display learning, not to impress, not to translate — it is to give every Christian the door to the original Word.

mc.stem: In John 1:1 ('In the beginning was the Word'), what is the Greek word translated 'Word,' and why is its meaning richer than the English suggests?
options: The Greek word is LOGOS (Strong's G3056), which means more than 'a single spoken word' — in Greek philosophy it meant the rational principle that holds the universe together, the logic of the cosmos; John applied this rich word to Jesus Christ Himself
The Greek word is RHEMA, which simply means 'sound'
The Greek word is LALEO, which means 'to speak'
The Greek word is GRAMMA, which means 'letter of the alphabet'
mc.why: John deliberately picked the Greek word LOGOS, which carried enormous philosophical weight in the Greek world. To his Greek-speaking readers, logos was the rational principle that ordered the cosmos — the LOGIC behind reality itself. John says: that very Logos became flesh and dwelt among us. Jesus Christ is the rational principle behind the universe, now walking in Galilee. None of that is visible in the English 'Word' alone. We will study logos in depth in Unit 8.

mc.stem: Why is John 1:1 chosen as the anchor scripture of this entire Language Appreciation course?
options: Because it is the most frequently quoted verse in modern hymns
Because it is the shortest verse in the New Testament

Because the verse is itself about words and the Word — it teaches that God's revelation is verbal, that Christ Himself is the Word, and the whole Bible is one Book, one Hero, one Story pointing to Him — every Hebrew and Greek letter studied in this course is finally a road sign pointing to the Logos
Because it was the first verse John ever wrote
mc.why: John 1:1 anchors the course for three reasons. First, the verse is itself about words: God's revelation is verbal, and Christ Himself is the Word. Second, the verse is impossible to fully understand from English alone; the Greek LOGOS carries layers no English word fully captures. Third, the verse closes the loop: every Greek letter and Hebrew letter you learn in this course finally points to the same Word, who is Christ. The Bible is one Book, one Hero, one Story — and the Hero is Jesus, the Logos of John 1:1.

mc.stem: In what order does the eleven-unit roadmap proceed?
options: Greek alphabet first, then Hebrew, then Strong's, then capstone
All eleven units cover Strong's numbers in detail
Units jump randomly between Hebrew and Greek with no clear sequence

Unit 1 (why) → Units 2–5 (Hebrew alphabet, vowels, word treasures) → Units 6–9 (Greek alphabet, four foundational words, four salvation words) → Unit 10 (Strong's numbers) → Unit 11 (capstone word study)
mc.why: The course follows the natural pedagogical order: orientation first (Unit 1), then Hebrew (Units 2-5: alphabet, vowels, roots, word treasures), then Greek (Units 6-9: alphabet first half, alphabet second half, four foundational words logos/agapê/charis/pneuma, four salvation words pistis/sôzô/dikaiosynê/kyrios), then the Strong's number bridge tool (Unit 10), then a capstone word study (Unit 11). Each unit builds on the one before; you must pass each unit's exam with 90% to advance to the next.

mc.stem: How should we understand the Bible as a whole?
options: As one Book, one Hero, one Story — with Jesus Christ as the Hero, the Logos of John 1:1, to whom every Hebrew letter and Greek word in Scripture is finally a road sign pointing
As 66 independent religious documents that should be studied in isolation from one another
As a book whose primary value is moral instruction for daily living
As a Hebrew document with Greek translations appended at the end
mc.why: Scripture is one unified Book, one Hero, one Story — with Jesus Christ as the Hero from Genesis to Revelation. This Christocentric reading is the devotional voice of the Language Appreciation course. Every Greek and Hebrew word you will learn is finally a road sign pointing to the same Christ, the Logos of John 1:1.

mc.stem: Why does the course conclude that learning the Hebrew and Greek alphabets is 'coming home' for any Western Bible reader, regardless of his nationality?
options: Because Hebrew is taught in all Western elementary schools
Because most Westerners have Jewish ancestry
Because Greek is the official language of all Christian denominations

Because every Western alphabet (English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, etc.) descends from Greek (alpha-beta), which itself descends from Hebrew/Phoenician (aleph-bet) — learning the original biblical alphabets is recovering the parent script of every Western tongue
mc.why: The English word 'alphabet' itself comes from Greek 'alpha' + 'beta,' which come from Hebrew 'aleph' + 'bet.' Every Western alphabet on earth — English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Greek, Russian, Coptic — descends from the Hebrew/Phoenician parent script. When you sit down to learn Hebrew and Greek, you are not learning two foreign alphabets; you are recovering the great-grandfather of your own letters. The course covers this in detail in Unit 2.

In Greek philosophy the logos was the rational ____ that holds the universe together.
